claim: A forward genetic screen of chemically mutagenized flies identified a short-sleeping mutant named redeye (rye).
source: In this study, we report a new protein involved in the homeostatic regulation of sleep in Drosophila. We conducted a forward genetic screen of chemically mutagenized flies to identify short-sleeping mutants and found one, redeye (rye) that shows a severe reduction of sleep length.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that a forward genetic screen was conducted and identified the rye mutant.

claim: The redeye (rye) mutant shows a severe reduction of sleep length.
source: We conducted a forward genetic screen of chemically mutagenized flies to identify short-sleeping mutants and found one, redeye (rye) that shows a severe reduction of sleep length.
evidence: The abstract and results section provide behavioral data showing reduced sleep in rye mutants.

claim: The rye gene encodes a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor α subunit.
source: Cloning of rye reveals that it encodes a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor α subunit required for Drosophila sleep.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by molecular cloning and sequencing data in the results.

claim: RYE is required for Drosophila sleep.
source: Cloning of rye reveals that it encodes a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor α subunit required for Drosophila sleep.
evidence: The abstract states this requirement, supported by mutant phenotype data.

claim: Levels of RYE oscillate in light-dark cycles.
source: Levels of RYE oscillate in light–dark cycles and peak at times of daily sleep.
evidence: The abstract states this, and western blot data in Figure 6B shows oscillating RYE protein levels.

claim: RYE levels peak at times of daily sleep.
source: Levels of RYE oscillate in light–dark cycles and peak at times of daily sleep.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 6B shows peaks at ZT6-10 and ZT18-22, corresponding to sleep times.

claim: Cycling of RYE is independent of a functional circadian clock.
source: Cycling of RYE is independent of a functional circadian clock, but rather depends upon the sleep homeostat, as protein levels are up-regulated in short-sleeping mutants and also in wild type animals following sleep deprivation.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 6C shows RYE cycling persists in Clkjrk mutants lacking a functional clock.

claim: RYE cycling depends upon the sleep homeostat.
source: Cycling of RYE is independent of a functional circadian clock, but rather depends upon the sleep homeostat, as protein levels are up-regulated in short-sleeping mutants and also in wild type animals following sleep deprivation.
evidence: The abstract states this, supported by data showing RYE upregulation in short-sleeping mutants and after sleep deprivation.

claim: RYE protein levels are up-regulated in short-sleeping mutants.
source: Cycling of RYE is independent of a functional circadian clock, but rather depends upon the sleep homeostat, as protein levels are up-regulated in short-sleeping mutants and also in wild type animals following sleep deprivation.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 7 shows elevated RYE levels in fumin, sss, and insomniac mutants.

claim: RYE protein levels are up-regulated in wild type animals following sleep deprivation.
source: Cycling of RYE is independent of a functional circadian clock, but rather depends upon the sleep homeostat, as protein levels are up-regulated in short-sleeping mutants and also in wild type animals following sleep deprivation.
evidence: The abstract states this, and Figure 8A shows high RYE levels immediately following sleep deprivation.

claim: The homeostatic drive to sleep increases levels of RYE.
source: We propose that the homeostatic drive to sleep increases levels of RYE, which responds to this drive by promoting sleep.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that RYE levels increase with sleep deprivation and in short-sleeping mutants.

claim: RYE responds to homeostatic drive by promoting sleep.
source: We propose that the homeostatic drive to sleep increases levels of RYE, which responds to this drive by promoting sleep.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that rye mutants have reduced sleep and RYE expression rescues the phenotype.

claim: Sleep is a common and prominent behavior in almost all vertebrate animals and most invertebrates.
source: Sleep is a common and prominent behavior in almost all vertebrate animals and also in most invertebrates (Cirelli, 2009; Sehgal and Mignot, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Prolonged sleep deprivation can lead to death.
source: The function of sleep is a mystery, but it is surely of great importance to animals, as prolonged sleep deprivation can lead to death.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Anatomical studies in mammals and birds have revealed brain structures and neurotransmitters that regulate sleep and wakefulness.
source: Anatomical studies in mammals and birds have revealed brain structures and neurotransmitters that regulate sleep and wakefulness (Saper et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian counterparts of some sleep components identified in model organisms also regulate sleep.
source: Mammalian counterparts of some sleep components identified in these model animals also regulate sleep (Joho et al., 2006), which argues that (i) behavioral genetics in lower organisms provides an efficient tool to identify sleep components, (ii) at least some of the mechanisms underlying sleep are conserved through evolution.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Behavioral genetics in lower organisms provides an efficient tool to identify sleep components.
source: Mammalian counterparts of some sleep components identified in these model animals also regulate sleep (Joho et al., 2006), which argues that (i) behavioral genetics in lower organisms provides an efficient tool to identify sleep components, (ii) at least some of the mechanisms underlying sleep are conserved through evolution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that sleep components are conserved across species.

claim: At least some of the mechanisms underlying sleep are conserved through evolution.
source: Mammalian counterparts of some sleep components identified in these model animals also regulate sleep (Joho et al., 2006), which argues that (i) behavioral genetics in lower organisms provides an efficient tool to identify sleep components, (ii) at least some of the mechanisms underlying sleep are conserved through evolution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that sleep components are conserved across species.

claim: A two-process model for sleep regulation has been widely accepted by the sleep field.
source: A two-process model for sleep regulation has been widely accepted by the sleep field.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Process C (the circadian clock) controls the timing of sleep onset and offset.
source: Process C (the circadian clock) controls the timing, in other words the onset and offset of sleep, whereas process S (the sleep homeostat) regulates sleep duration based on the sleep pressure built up during prior wakefulness (Borbely, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the two-process model.

claim: Process S (the sleep homeostat) regulates sleep duration based on the sleep pressure built up during prior wakefulness.
source: Process C (the circadian clock) controls the timing, in other words the onset and offset of sleep, whereas process S (the sleep homeostat) regulates sleep duration based on the sleep pressure built up during prior wakefulness (Borbely, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the two-process model.

claim: Molecular mechanisms of circadian control have been well characterized.
source: Molecular mechanisms of circadian control have been well characterized (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012), but, as noted above, relatively little is known about process S.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Relatively little is known about process S (the sleep homeostat).
source: Molecular mechanisms of circadian control have been well characterized (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012), but, as noted above, relatively little is known about process S.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Forward genetic screens in Drosophila have led to the identification of several mutants with altered sleep length.
source: Forward genetic screens in Drosophila have led to the identification of several mutants with altered sleep length, but while the genes implicated by these mutants are required for implementation of sleep drive, they have not yet been directly linked to this drive (Sehgal and Mignot, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Genes implicated by sleep mutants are required for implementation of sleep drive but have not yet been directly linked to this drive.
source: Forward genetic screens in Drosophila have led to the identification of several mutants with altered sleep length, but while the genes implicated by these mutants are required for implementation of sleep drive, they have not yet been directly linked to this drive (Sehgal and Mignot, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The rye mutation maps to a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR).
source: The rye mutation maps to a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR), which interacts with a previously identified sleep-regulating protein, SLEEPLESS (SSS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by molecular mapping data in the results.

claim: RYE interacts with SLEEPLESS (SSS), a previously identified sleep-regulating protein.
source: The rye mutation maps to a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR), which interacts with a previously identified sleep-regulating protein, SLEEPLESS (SSS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by genetic interaction and electrophysiology data in the results.

claim: Homeostatic sleep drive promotes sleep at least in part by increasing expression of RYE.
source: We conclude that homeostatic sleep drive promotes sleep at least in part by increasing expression of RYE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that RYE levels increase with sleep deprivation and in short-sleeping mutants.

claim: Sleep amounts were normally distributed in the 1857 lines assayed in the forward genetic screen.
source: As seen in previous screens (Koh et al., 2008), sleep amounts were normally distributed in the 1857 lines assayed (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A histogram.

claim: Two homozygous mutant lines showed a severe reduction of sleep length in the screen.
source: Two homozygous mutant lines showed a severe reduction of sleep length, and we focused on one of these that we named redeye (rye).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the screen outcome.

claim: rye homozygotes show a >50% reduction in both daytime and night-time sleep.
source: rye homozygotes show a >50% reduction in both daytime and night-time sleep (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and quantified in Figure 1C.

claim: The activity of rye mutants is comparable with that of wild type controls.
source: The activity (average number of beam crossings during periods of activity) of rye mutants is comparable with that of wild type controls, suggesting it is not a hyperactive mutant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: rye is not a hyperactive mutant.
source: The activity (average number of beam crossings during periods of activity) of rye mutants is comparable with that of wild type controls, suggesting it is not a hyperactive mutant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that activity levels are normal in rye mutants.

claim: rye heterozygotes have slightly less sleep than wild type.
source: rye heterozygotes have slightly less sleep than wild type, suggesting that the rye mutation is partially dominant (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The rye mutation is partially dominant.
source: rye heterozygotes have slightly less sleep than wild type, suggesting that the rye mutation is partially dominant (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype.

claim: The dramatic reduction of baseline sleep in rye mutants results largely from a shortening of the average sleep episode duration.
source: The dramatic reduction of baseline sleep results largely from a shortening of the average sleep episode duration (Figure 1D), which is indicative of a defect in sleep maintenance.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Shortened sleep episode duration in rye mutants is indicative of a defect in sleep maintenance.
source: The dramatic reduction of baseline sleep results largely from a shortening of the average sleep episode duration (Figure 1D), which is indicative of a defect in sleep maintenance.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that sleep episodes are shorter.

claim: The average number of sleep episodes at night is increased significantly in rye mutants.
source: The average number of sleep episodes at night is actually increased significantly in rye mutants, perhaps because the sleep homeostat senses sleep loss and compensates by initiating more bouts.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The sleep homeostat may sense sleep loss in rye mutants and compensate by initiating more sleep bouts.
source: The average number of sleep episodes at night is actually increased significantly in rye mutants, perhaps because the sleep homeostat senses sleep loss and compensates by initiating more bouts.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the increased number of sleep episodes.

claim: rye mutants did not lose much additional sleep in response to mechanical stimulation in sleep deprivation assays.
source: We also assayed rye mutants in sleep deprivation assays and found that they did not lose much additional sleep in response to mechanical stimulation (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text, though the data is not shown.

claim: An inability to sustain sleep bouts leads to the buildup of high sleep need in rye mutants, which makes them resist further sleep loss.
source: We surmise that an inability to sustain sleep bouts leads to the buildup of high sleep need in rye mutants, which makes them resist any further sleep loss.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that rye mutants are resistant to sleep deprivation.

claim: rye mutants display robust rest:activity rhythms in constant darkness (∼62% rhythmicity).
source: rye mutants display robust rest:activity rhythms in DD (∼62% rhythmicity) despite showing prolonged duration of activity (Figure 2A; Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Most rye homozygotes are rhythmic in constant darkness.
source: Thus, most rye homozygotes are rhythmic.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the rhythmicity data in constant darkness.

claim: Circadian cycling of the clock protein PERIOD (PER) is normal in central clock cells of rye mutants.
source: Consistent with the intact circadian behavior, circadian cycling of the clock protein, PERIOD (PER), is normal in central clock cells of rye mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only the homeostatic regulation of sleep is affected in rye mutants.
source: We conclude that only the homeostatic regulation of sleep is affected in rye mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that circadian rhythms are normal but sleep is reduced.

claim: Deep-sequencing identified many nucleotide changes in the rye background relative to the parental control.
source: Despite starting with a newly isogenized line, deep-sequencing identified many nucleotide changes in the rye background relative to the parental control and so considerable mapping was required to pinpoint the relevant mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the mapping strategy.

claim: Meiotic recombination analysis positioned rye between two genetic markers, thread and curled, in the centromeric region of the 3rd chromosome.
source: Meiotic recombination analysis positioned rye between two genetic markers, thread and curled, in the centromeric region of the 3rd chromosome.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Further mapping studies narrowed down the rye locus to ∼11 mega-bases.
source: Further mapping studies, using self identified single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers, narrowed it down to ∼11 mega-bases (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Within the 11 Mb region, there were 1457 potential mutations, but only nine that produced an amino-acid change in coding regions.
source: Within the 11 Mb region identified through recombination mapping, there were 1457 potential mutations, but only nine that produced an amino-acid change in coding regions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the sequencing analysis.

claim: A C-T transition in CG12414 leads to a threonine to methionine change and is present only in rye mutants.
source: The last of the nine changes identified by deep-sequencing was a C-T transition (typical for EMS-induced mutations) that leads to a threonine to methionine change in CG12414 and is present only in rye mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CG12414 encodes an α subunit of a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR).
source: CG12414 encodes an α subunit of a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) (Lansdell and Millar, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The predicted RYE protein is homologous to several nAChR subunits, including α3, α2, α6, α4 and α7 in order of similarity.
source: The predicted protein is homologous to several nAChR subunits, including α3, α2, α6, α4 and α7 in order of similarity.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on sequence analysis.

claim: The rye mutation is at the junction between the ligand binding domain (LBD) and the trans-membrane domain (TM).
source: Alignment of CG12414 with α3 and α7 using the ClustalW2 algorithm shows that the rye mutation is at the junction between the LBD and the trans-membrane domain (TM) (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The junction region between LBD and TM is highly conserved across species.
source: Interestingly, this junction region is highly conserved across species and the specific threonine mutated in rye is conserved in all α7 subunits (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D alignment.

claim: The specific threonine mutated in rye is conserved in all α7 subunits.
source: Interestingly, this junction region is highly conserved across species and the specific threonine mutated in rye is conserved in all α7 subunits (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D alignment.

claim: The rye promoter driving RYE expression (ryeP > uas-rye) partially rescued the rye mutant phenotype.
source: While either transgene alone did not alter the rye short sleep phenotype, the rye promoter driving RYE expression (ryeP > uas-rye) partially rescued the mutant phenotype and restored total sleep to levels seen in rye heterozygotes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ryeP > uas-rye does not increase sleep length in a wild type background.
source: In a wild type background, ryeP > uas-rye does not increase sleep length (data not shown), suggesting that the increase in sleep is specific to the mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the text, though the data is not shown.

claim: The increase in sleep from ryeP > uas-rye is specific to the rye mutant.
source: In a wild type background, ryeP > uas-rye does not increase sleep length (data not shown), suggesting that the increase in sleep is specific to the mutant.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the transgene only increases sleep in the mutant background.

claim: Knockdown of RYE expression through RNA interference reduces total sleep length.
source: Levels of RYE were reduced (Figure 4D), as was the total sleep length (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: ryeT227M is a loss-of-function mutation.
source: Since ryeT227M reduces sleep as well (Figure 1), these data suggest that the T227M mutant allele causes loss of RYE function.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that both the mutation and RNAi knockdown reduce sleep.

claim: ryeT227M may be a dominant-negative mutation.
source: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor forms a pentameric structure, consisting of five homo-oligomeric or hetero-oligomeric subunits (Miwa et al., 2011), so a dominant negative mutation in any one subunit may well interfere with activity of the complex.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the pentameric structure of nAChRs and the partial dominance of the mutation.

claim: rye heterozygotes carrying a genomic sss transgene showed a further reduction of sleep.
source: While transheterozygotes of rye and sss (sss/+; rye/+) showed sleep duration comparable to that of rye/+ alone (data not shown), rye heterozygotes carrying a genomic sss transgene, which increases SSS expression above that of wild type controls, showed a further reduction of sleep (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of the sss transgene on sleep in rye heterozygotes was observed with three independent insertions.
source: The effect was observed with three independent insertions of the sss transgene, indicating that it was not due to insertion site effects (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The sss transgene does not have a significant effect on sleep in wild type flies.
source: We note that this sss transgene does not have a significant effect on sleep in wild type flies although it completely rescues the sleep phenotype of sss mutants (Koh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The effect of the sss transgene on sleep is specific to rye mutants.
source: Thus, the effect is specific to rye mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that the transgene only affects sleep in the rye background.

claim: SSS is a GPI-anchored protein that regulates the Shaker potassium channel.
source: SSS is a GPI-anchored protein that regulates the Shaker potassium channel and its predicted structure resembles that of a specific class of toxins (Wu et al., 2010; Dean et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The predicted structure of SSS resembles that of a specific class of toxins.
source: SSS is a GPI-anchored protein that regulates the Shaker potassium channel and its predicted structure resembles that of a specific class of toxins (Wu et al., 2010; Dean et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SSS is most similar to the mammalian Lynx-1 protein.
source: It is most similar to the mammalian Lynx-1 protein, which is known to inhibit activity of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (Miwa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Lynx-1 is known to inhibit activity of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
source: It is most similar to the mammalian Lynx-1 protein, which is known to inhibit activity of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (Miwa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: SSS exacerbated the phenotype of flies heterozygous for rye.
source: The fact that SSS exacerbated the phenotype of flies heterozygous for rye, which have reduced activity of nAChR, suggested that SSS also regulates nAChRs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: SSS also regulates nAChRs.
source: The fact that SSS exacerbated the phenotype of flies heterozygous for rye, which have reduced activity of nAChR, suggested that SSS also regulates nAChRs.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic interaction data.

claim: Heterologous expression of SSS reduces current following ACh application in Xenopus oocytes expressing Drosophila RYE and human nAChR β2.
source: However, we still detected a significant reduction of nAChR current upon co-expression with SSS (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SSS inhibits the robust current produced by the human α4β2 receptor complex.
source: We also co-expressed in vitro transcribed sss and human α4 and β2 subunits and found that SSS also inhibits the robust current produced by the human receptor complex (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SSS may promote wake by repressing activity of nAChRs.
source: Thus, in addition to its sleep-promoting role reported previously, SSS may also promote wake by repressing activity of nAChRs.
evidence: This is an inference from the electrophysiology data showing SSS inhibits nAChR currents.

claim: Loss of the sleep-promoting role of SSS has a dominant effect in sss mutants.
source: As discussed below, loss of the sleep-promoting role has a dominant effect in sss mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an interpretation of the data.

claim: rye mRNA levels are constant over the course of the day.
source: While period (per), a well-known circadian clock component, oscillates with a circadian rhythm (Zheng and Sehgal, 2012), rye mRNA levels were found to be constant (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: RYE protein shows a robust rhythm with two peaks each day, one at around ZT6-10 and the other at ZT18-22.
source: Surprisingly, in contrast to the flat mRNA levels, levels of RYE protein show a robust rhythm with two peaks each day, one at around ZT6-10 and the other at ZT18-22 (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The two daily peaks of RYE correspond to the two daily times of sleep, the afternoon siesta and night-time sleep.
source: Interestingly, these correspond to the two daily times of sleep, the afternoon siesta and night-time sleep (Figure 1B), suggesting that RYE is expressed in phase with sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from comparing Figures 1B and 6B.

claim: RYE is expressed in phase with sleep.
source: Interestingly, these correspond to the two daily times of sleep, the afternoon siesta and night-time sleep (Figure 1B), suggesting that RYE is expressed in phase with sleep.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that RYE peaks coincide with sleep times.

claim: The cycling of RYE persists in constant darkness.
source: The cycling of RYE persists in constant darkness, as do rhythms of sleep (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text, though the data is not shown.

claim: RYE continues to cycle in Clkjrk flies that lack a circadian clock.
source: Furthermore, we found that RYE continues to cycle in Clkjrk flies that lack a circadian clock, although the phase of RYE expression tends to be more variable in these flies (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The phase of RYE expression tends to be more variable in Clkjrk flies.
source: Furthermore, we found that RYE continues to cycle in Clkjrk flies that lack a circadian clock, although the phase of RYE expression tends to be more variable in these flies (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The RYE oscillation per se does not require process C (the circadian clock).
source: These data suggest that the RYE oscillation per se does not require process C of the two process model, but may depend upon process S (sleep homeostasis).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that RYE cycles in clock mutants.

claim: RYE oscillation may depend upon process S (sleep homeostasis).
source: These data suggest that the RYE oscillation per se does not require process C of the two process model, but may depend upon process S (sleep homeostasis).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that RYE cycles in clock mutants but is affected by sleep state.

claim: The circadian clock may function to provide more precise timing of RYE expression.
source: However, the circadian clock may function to provide more precise timing of RYE expression, perhaps through its control of sleep onset and offset.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that RYE phase is more variable in clock mutants.

claim: Overall RYE values are higher in fumin mutants than in wild type controls.
source: While RYE still cycles in fumin, the mean value of all six daily time points from three independent experiments (n = 3) shows that overall levels of RYE are higher than in wild type controls (Figure 7—source data 1). *p<0.05.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Overall RYE values are higher in sss mutants than in wild type controls.
source: As in A, the quantification reflects the mean across the day from three independent experiments (n = 3). *p<0.05.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Overall RYE values are higher in insomniac mutants than in wild type controls.
source: Quantification as above (n = 3). *p<0.05.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: RYE reflects sleep need.
source: Based upon these data, we suggest that RYE reflects sleep need.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that RYE is elevated in short-sleeping mutants.

claim: RYE is elevated at the time of sleep onset.
source: It is elevated at the time of sleep onset and is further increased in short-sleeping mutants because they have high sleep need.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the RYE cycling data.

claim: RYE is further increased in short-sleeping mutants because they have high sleep need.
source: It is elevated at the time of sleep onset and is further increased in short-sleeping mutants because they have high sleep need.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the elevated RYE in short-sleeping mutants.

claim: Sleep-deprived flies had high levels of RYE immediately following deprivation (ZT0).
source: RYE levels were assayed during the 5 hr sleep rebound window. In the non-deprived control, RYE levels were low at ZT0 and high at ZT5, as noted above. Sleep-deprived flies had high levels of RYE immediately following deprivation (ZT0), but levels were low at ZT5 (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: RYE levels were low at ZT5 in sleep-deprived flies.
source: Sleep-deprived flies had high levels of RYE immediately following deprivation (ZT0), but levels were low at ZT5 (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The RYE profile fits the profile for sleep drive, which is expected to be high at the end of deprivation, but then dissipated over the course of rebound sleep.
source: This fits the profile for sleep drive, which is expected to be high at the end of deprivation, but then dissipated over the course of rebound sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sleep deprivation data.

claim: RYE is required to maintain sleep.
source: We show that RYE not only reflects sleep drive, but is also required for sleep maintenance (Figures 1, 4 and 8).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by mutant and rescue data.

claim: Transgenic expression of rye in a wild type background does not increase sleep.
source: However, transgenic expression of rye in a wild type background does not increase sleep, suggesting that while rye is necessary, it is not sufficient for sleep onset.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: RYE is necessary but not sufficient for sleep onset.
source: However, transgenic expression of rye in a wild type background does not increase sleep, suggesting that while rye is necessary, it is not sufficient for sleep onset.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that overexpression does not increase sleep.

claim: RYE is not part of the homeostat, but immediately downstream of it.
source: For the moment, though, we prefer the parsimonious explanation noted above, that RYE is not part of the homeostat, but immediately downstream of it.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' preferred interpretation.

claim: Acetylcholine signaling has been long proposed as an arousal factor.
source: Acetylcholine signaling has been long proposed as an arousal factor, as the nAChR complex is a cation channel that normally promotes neuronal activity and ACh is released during wakefulness in mammals (Platt and Riedel, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: The nAChR complex is a cation channel that normally promotes neuronal activity.
source: Acetylcholine signaling has been long proposed as an arousal factor, as the nAChR complex is a cation channel that normally promotes neuronal activity and ACh is released during wakefulness in mammals (Platt and Riedel, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: ACh is released during wakefulness in mammals.
source: Acetylcholine signaling has been long proposed as an arousal factor, as the nAChR complex is a cation channel that normally promotes neuronal activity and ACh is released during wakefulness in mammals (Platt and Riedel, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: At least one nAChR subunit (RYE) promotes sleep in the fly.
source: In contrast, our study indicates that at least one nAChR subunit (RYE) promotes sleep in the fly.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study.

claim: RYE may be expressed specifically in sleep promoting neurons.
source: One possibility is that RYE is expressed specifically in sleep promoting neurons, while other subunits of AChRs are in wake-promoting cells.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the sleep-promoting role of RYE.

claim: An increase in ACh during wakefulness may contribute to the accumulation of sleep drive and to the increase in RYE.
source: An increase in ACh during wakefulness may contribute to the accumulation of sleep drive and to the increase in RYE (Lindstrom, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a possible mechanism and supported by a citation.

claim: SSS was previously identified as a sleep promoting factor, essential for maintaining baseline sleep and for homeostatic rebound.
source: SSS was previously identified as a sleep promoting factor, essential for maintaining baseline sleep and for homeostatic rebound (Koh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of SSS promotes wakefulness in ryeT227M heterozygotes.
source: What is surprising is that overexpression of SSS promotes wakefulness in ryeT227M heterozygotes (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: SSS acts like a brake on nAChR (RYE) activity.
source: In this study, we report that SSS acts like a brake on nAChR (RYE) activity (Figure 5C,D), as does Lynx-1, a SSS-like molecule, in mammals (Miwa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The overall effect of SSS is to promote sleep.
source: As both sssP1 (a null mutation) and sssP2 (a hypomorphic allele) are short-sleeping mutants (Koh et al., 2008), we propose that the overall effect of SSS is to promote sleep.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The reduced sleep in sss mutants probably results from an increase of neuronal excitability, through inactivation of potassium channels (Shaker), or from hyperactivity of nAChR channels in wake-promoting neurons.
source: The reduced sleep in sss mutants probably results from an increase of neuronal excitability, through inactivation of potassium channels (Shaker) (Dean et al., 2011), or from hyperactivity of nAChR channels in wake-promoting neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism and supported by a citation.

claim: The sleep-inhibiting effect of SSS, mediated through RYE, is masked by other more dominant influences in typical conditions.
source: Thus, typically the sleep-inhibiting effect of SSS, mediated through RYE, is masked by these other more dominant influences.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: In a sensitized background (i.e., rye/+), the sleep-inhibiting effect of SSS is evident.
source: However, in a sensitized background (i.e., rye/+), this effect is evident.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the genetic interaction data.

claim: Genes identified through independent genetic screens in Drosophila are turning out to interact with one another.
source: It is interesting that genes identified through independent genetic screens in Drosophila are turning out to interact with one another.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the field.

claim: SSS and Shaker were isolated independently as sleep-regulating genes and subsequently shown to interact.
source: SSS and Shaker were isolated independently as sleep-regulating genes (Cirelli et al., 2005; Koh et al., 2008), and subsequently shown to interact, and now we find that RYE interacts with SSS.
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RYE interacts with SSS.
source: SSS and Shaker were isolated independently as sleep-regulating genes (Cirelli et al., 2005; Koh et al., 2008), and subsequently shown to interact, and now we find that RYE interacts with SSS.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the current study.

claim: Genetic approaches are converging upon specific sleep-regulating pathways.
source: Given that each of these genes represents a relatively infrequent hit in an unbiased screen, the interactions suggest that genetic approaches are converging upon specific sleep-regulating pathways.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that independently identified genes interact.

claim: A recent GWAS study for sleep-altering loci in humans identified significant effects of SNPs in an nAchR subunit as well as in a regulatory subunit of Shaker.
source: Interestingly, a recent GWAS study for sleep-altering loci in humans identified significant effects of SNPs in an nAchR subunit as well as in a regulatory subunit of Shaker, suggesting that these mechanisms are also conserved across species (Allebrandt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to a GWAS study.

claim: Sleep-regulating mechanisms involving nAChR and Shaker are conserved across species.
source: Interestingly, a recent GWAS study for sleep-altering loci in humans identified significant effects of SNPs in an nAchR subunit as well as in a regulatory subunit of Shaker, suggesting that these mechanisms are also conserved across species (Allebrandt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the GWAS data showing similar loci in humans.

claim: RYE represents a molecular correlate of delta power.
source: We suggest that RYE represents a molecular correlate of delta power, a characteristic of an electroencephalogram (EEG) that reflects sleep drive.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the properties of RYE.

claim: Delta power is a characteristic of an electroencephalogram (EEG) that reflects sleep drive.
source: We suggest that RYE represents a molecular correlate of delta power, a characteristic of an electroencephalogram (EEG) that reflects sleep drive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: A few other molecules were reported to change with sleep drive, but the effects were at the level of the mRNA.
source: Recently, a few other molecules were reported to change with sleep drive, but the effects were at the level of the mRNA, the magnitude of the increase was less than we report here for RYE and loss of the molecules did not affect baseline sleep duration (Seugnet et al., 2006; Maret et al., 2007; Naidoo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The magnitude of the increase in other sleep drive molecules was less than reported for RYE.
source: Recently, a few other molecules were reported to change with sleep drive, but the effects were at the level of the mRNA, the magnitude of the increase was less than we report here for RYE and loss of the molecules did not affect baseline sleep duration (Seugnet et al., 2006; Maret et al., 2007; Naidoo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous work.

claim: Loss of other sleep drive molecules did not affect baseline sleep duration.
source: Recently, a few other molecules were reported to change with sleep drive, but the effects were at the level of the mRNA, the magnitude of the increase was less than we report here for RYE and loss of the molecules did not affect baseline sleep duration (Seugnet et al., 2006; Maret et al., 2007; Naidoo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Insomniac is a component of specific protein degradation pathways in the cell.
source: It is worth noting that a recently identified sleep regulator, Insomniac, is a component of specific protein degradation pathways in the cell (Stavropoulos and Young, 2011).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: RYE cycling does not require Insomniac.
source: Although our study indicates that RYE cycling does not require Insomniac (Figure 7C), it is possible that it is regulated by other protein turn-over machinery.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: RYE may be regulated by other protein turn-over machinery.
source: Although our study indicates that RYE cycling does not require Insomniac (Figure 7C), it is possible that it is regulated by other protein turn-over machinery.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility.

claim: Translational/posttranslational regulation appears to be part of the mechanism of sleep homeostasis.
source: Thus, translational/posttranslational regulation appears to be part of the mechanism of sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the observation that RYE cycles at the protein level.

claim: RYE does not accumulate gradually over the wake period in a daily cycle.
source: However, while RYE builds up during sleep deprivation, it does not accumulate gradually over the wake period in a daily cycle.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the RYE cycling data.

claim: RYE displays a marked increase close to the time of sleep onset.
source: Rather, it displays a marked increase close to the time of sleep onset, suggesting that it is not a central component of the homeostat, but responds to an upstream homeostatic signal, perhaps when that signal reaches a certain threshold.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the RYE cycling data.

claim: RYE responds to an upstream homeostatic signal, perhaps when that signal reaches a certain threshold.
source: Rather, it displays a marked increase close to the time of sleep onset, suggesting that it is not a central component of the homeostat, but responds to an upstream homeostatic signal, perhaps when that signal reaches a certain threshold.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the timing of RYE increases.

claim: Over-expression of RYE does not promote sleep.
source: The fact that over-expression of RYE does not promote sleep also supports the idea that it is not the sleep-inducing homeostatic signal (further discussed below).
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: RYE is not simply a sleep output gene or sleep biomarker.
source: Nevertheless, RYE is not simply a sleep output gene or sleep biomarker.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: RYE is required for implementation of signals from the homeostat.
source: It is required for implementation of signals from the homeostat and it functions to maintain sleep.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutant and rescue data.

claim: RYE functions to maintain sleep.
source: It is required for implementation of signals from the homeostat and it functions to maintain sleep.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutant phenotype data.

claim: rye is a sleep-regulating gene immediately downstream of the homeostat.
source: Thus, we propose that rye is a sleep-regulating gene immediately downstream of the homeostat.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed model.
